supersedes_note: Third sample of the same workload on the same machine and date. It supersedes the v3 re-measurement because v3 was taken while several unrelated heavy compile jobs were running on this box, which depressed every figure. v3 is retained for provenance: the discrepancy between v2, v3, and v4 is itself the finding, and is the reason background CPU load is now recorded per run.
run_admission_criteria: Fewer than ~5,000 TIME_WAIT entries at run start (see socket_pressure_finding).
Whole-machine CPU utilisation sampled immediately before each run and recorded, because it turned out to dominate the result.

background_load_finding.note: The dominant source of variance on this machine is not the server, the socket state, or CPU power management. It is unrelated CPU load. This was found by re-running the byte-identical binary after unrelated compile jobs finished and getting figures roughly 75% higher than v3.
background_load_finding.observed: Across the runs in this artifact, whole-machine CPU utilisation sampled at run start ranged from ~19% to ~62%, and throughput tracked it closely: the three runs starting under 25% CPU returned 2,440-2,803 req/s, while the two starting above 60% returned 1,840-1,941 req/s.
background_load_finding.implication: A benchmark taken on a shared or busy developer machine can be wrong by a factor of ~1.5 while reporting zero errors and a plausible-looking number. Record the machine's load alongside the result, or the artifact cannot be interpreted later. This is why v3's medians are superseded rather than merely re-averaged with these.

socket_pressure_finding.note: Carried forward from v3 and still valid. Throughput degrades monotonically as TIME_WAIT accumulates, well BEFORE any connection errors appear, so a port-starved run silently reports a low number rather than failing.
socket_pressure_finding.observed: With TIME_WAIT above ~10,000, throughput fell to 244-400 req/s and p99 rose past 350 ms, with 0-17 errors.
socket_pressure_finding.implication: A run with zero errors is not automatically a valid run. Filter on starting socket pressure, not just on the absence of errors.

comparison_with_pre_async.note: Read with care. The pre-async baseline (windows-x86_64-2026-07-17.json) is a SINGLE run whose machine load was not recorded. Given that load moves this benchmark by ~1.5x, that baseline cannot support a precise A/B claim in either direction.
comparison_with_pre_async.throughput: The async median (2,139 req/s) is above the pre-async single sample (1,296) and the pre-async figure sits below this artifact's minimum (1,840). Directionally favourable, but not a clean A/B: the baseline's machine conditions are unknown.
comparison_with_pre_async.p50: Improved (11.081 ms to a median of 6.282 ms); the baseline sits outside this artifact's range.
comparison_with_pre_async.p95: Improved (20.213 ms to a median of 15.311 ms); ranges do not overlap.
comparison_with_pre_async.p99: Improved (39.151 ms to a median of 23.772 ms), though this artifact's max (43.721 ms) exceeds the baseline, so the tail is not uniformly better run to run.
comparison_with_pre_async.honest_summary: No throughput or latency win is claimed as a measured result, because the baseline is one unlabelled run. What the async migration is claimed to buy is cancellation safety, per-request deadlines, and not pinning an OS thread per waiting request.

measurement_caveats: Power-managed laptop with unpinned CPU clocks and unrelated background load; figures are envelopes, not point claims.
Loopback TCP/HTTP with one connection per request. Release compilation excluded.
No GPU, ONNX Runtime, or PyTorch execution was measured. Not a capacity or service-level claim.
